extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Office's Alice/Mayo framework (Step 1 statutory category; Step 2A/2B judicial-exception analysis). Focuses on claim construction (BRI), identifying judicial exceptions, and recognizing when claims are directed to technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory Category Determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter? Evaluation of this step should be made after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes: If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) the claim is non-statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES), proceed to analyze eligibility at Pathway A or Step 2A. Examiner should review the entire disclosure and apply BRI (see MPEP §2106, §2111) before concluding.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If BRI encompasses both statutory and non-statutory embodiments (e.g., machine-readable media covering both compact disc and transitory carrier waves), the claim fails Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Best practice: examiner should point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2: Judicial Exceptions Overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim falls within a statutory category, claims 'directed to nothing more than abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature' are not eligible for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judicial exceptions reflect concerns about preemption of basic tools of scientific and technological work. Preemption is the underlying concern but is not a standalone test. Use the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) to resolve judicial-exception issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception (recite vs involve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A asks: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature) or an abstract idea? A claim is directed to a judicial exception when a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite means the exception is set forth or described in claim language (examples: Diehr's explicit equation; Mayo's wherein clause). If the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) it is eligible at Pathway B; if it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) it requires further analysis at Step 2B to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself. Consider the claim as a whole when performing Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions, care should be taken not to parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, multiple mental-step manipulations of information should be considered a single abstract idea rather than multiple separate abstract ideas. However, if a claim recites multiple exceptions it is directed to at least one judicial exception and must be analyzed in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the claimed concept and compare to court-identified abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) the examiner believes may be an abstract idea), and (2) comparing the claimed concept to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to one or more concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts, conclude it is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES) and proceed to Step 2B. If not similar and no basis to conclude it is an abstract idea, find Step 2A: NO and the claim is eligible at Pathway B unless it recites another exception. Use comparisons to precedent (e.g., Alice, Bilski, Flook) rather than judicial descriptors alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are improvements in computer functionality or other technology are not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inventions pertaining to improvements in computer functionality or to improvements in other technologies are not abstract when appropriately claimed, and thus may be eligible at Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical considerations: the specification should disclose sufficient details so a skilled artisan recognizes the claimed invention as providing an improvement; the claim itself must reflect the improvement (covers a particular solution or particular way to achieve an outcome rather than merely claiming the idea). Examiners must give the claim its BRI and evaluate both claim and specification. Examples of eligible claims include Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization rules), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on 'improvement' arguments (caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every addition of a computer renders a claim an improvement in computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed process can be performed without a computer, it cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer. Mere automation of manual processes or increasing speed solely from a general-purpose computer's capabilities is insufficient to show an improvement. Mere implementation on conventional or generic components does not qualify. Examiners should consult MPEP §2106.05(a) for cases where claims did not reflect an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve improvement questions early when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the question of whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either Step 2A or Step 2B, examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is clearly an improvement in technology (e.g., Enfish), it may be eligible at Pathway A under streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not directed to an abstract idea. If unclear at Step 2A, the improvement may still contribute to eligibility under Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation requirement: involving vs reciting an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is based on or involves an abstract idea, but does not recite it, then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims that are based on organizing information using a tabular format or that modify internet hyperlink protocol to produce a hybrid webpage may involve abstract ideas but not recite them, and thus are not directed to abstract ideas (see Enfish, DDR Holdings). Non-limiting hypotheticals (printer, washing machine, earring sensor, BRCA1 sequencing method, BIOS loading method) illustrate claims that do not set forth or describe an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite an abstract idea but as a whole are directed to an improvement or do not tie up the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites an abstract idea, but the claim as a whole is directed to an improvement or otherwise clearly does not seek to tie up the abstract idea, then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a recitation of an abstract idea occurs, the overall claim may be eligible if it amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea (Step 2B analysis). The specification and claim must show a specific improvement or inventive concept that prevents preemption of the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is the underlying concern but not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's concern underlying the judicial exceptions is preemption — preventing patents from monopolizing basic tools of science and technology — but preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a preemptive claim may be ineligible, absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate eligibility. Thus, examiners must apply the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) rather than relying solely on preemption inquiries.
